title: From the Atacama Desert, straight to the center of our galaxy
caption: The Milky Way over the Atacama Desert near Cerro Armazones, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at the ELT site, Cerro Armazones, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: The Milky Way stretches across this night landscape in the Atacama Desert, a region that has hosted ESO's observatories since the 1960s and that was chosen as the site of the Extremely Large Telescope. Our galaxy is a disc, and here we see it exactly edge-on.

Looking toward its center, the galaxy's plane is crowded with a hundred thousand million stars, along with a great deal of gas and dust between them. The dust absorbs visible light and forms the prominent dark lanes crossing the bright band.

Follow one of those lanes, which seems to rise from the center of the Galaxy toward the top, and you reach a yellowish nebula around the star Antares, also called Alpha Scorpii. Next to it is a bluish nebula around Rho Ophiuchi. The center of the Galaxy is found in the direction of Sagittarius.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, which brings out the colored nebulae near Antares and Rho Ophiuchi that are hard to see unaided.

explore: The Extremely Large Telescope is described by ESO as the world's biggest eye on the sky. The photograph was taken by Gerhard Hüdepohl, looking toward the crowded central regions of our galaxy.
alt: The bright band of the Milky Way seen edge-on over a desert, crossed by dark dust lanes, with a yellowish and a bluish nebula near the top.
